A culture of western and central Europe, from about 2800 to 1800 BCE, named after its bell-shaped pottery drinking cups. The map shows it in 2000 BCE in Britain, France and the Low Countries.

Beaker graves often hold the same set of goods: a beaker, copper daggers, arrowheads, stone wrist guards for archers and gold ornaments. The style seems to have begun in Iberia and spread along the Atlantic coast and up the Rhine, together with copper working and probably new drinking customs.

In central Europe and Britain the Beaker spread was also a movement of people. Ancient DNA shows that Beaker groups carried ancestry from the steppe herders of the Yamnaya culture, by way of the Corded Ware culture, and that after reaching Britain around 2450 BCE they largely replaced the people who had built Stonehenge. The Amesbury Archer, buried near Stonehenge with rich goods, grew up in central Europe. The Beaker world gave way to Bronze Age cultures such as Únětice and the Nordic Bronze Age.
